One thing that's been brought up a couple of times but not really been discussed is the third icon, the 'whenever' one. While I don't really have an opinion on the start/end of turn icons, I really don't think 'whenever' is a good idea at all. For a start, it's replacing a lot less text - the word 'when' or 'whenever' instead of seven, and in fact you probably wouldn't even be able to remove the word without the sentence not making sense any more - meaning it will take up more space instead of less. Not a big deal, but still not ideal.

Further, I don't see how it would make the game any simpler. The start/end of turn icons have a clear 'when' about them; it's the start of the villain turn, so you scan her cards for SV icons. Whenever icons, on the other hand, can activate pretty much at any point, so you end up in the exact same situation we have now, except this time there are W icons all over the cards. There may be a minor benefit in having the icons as a reminder to check the card to see what the effect is and when it activates, but that's such a minor benefit that it's rather outweighed by the issues of inconsistency and over-iconning.

posts.name: arenson9
posts.cooked:
Agreed -- the discussion of what would make the game better is different than the discussion of what is a good/practical choice for Greater Than Games.

 

Re: A 'Whenever' icon. I agree that adding a token would not replace text, but actually end up using more card space. That's clearly a detriment, but I think it would be outweighed by the value of being able to tell at a glance that there are out-of-turn effects to be considered. As an aside, I think that out-of-turn effects cause the most work in the game by far. They are the reason that for a long time I was very unenthusiastic about playing Spite.

 

By the way, perhaps 'Whenever' is the wrong term and 'Out-of-turn' is more appropriate, such that we'd want an 'O' icon, rather than a 'W' icon.

 

It's possible, though, that what would be even better would be to identify a (hopefully!) small number of conditions and use different icons for each. Perhaps they would be things like 'Upon being attacked', 'Upon using a power', 'Upon playing a card', 'Upon drawing a card'. The big problem I see with this, though, is that the number of icons one must understand quickly grows to be more of an effort that just reading and understanding the cards.

 

Any game is easier to play, I think, when someone who knows it teaches it, rather than having to learn the game oneself. Sentinels is deceptively complex, because all of the complexity of the game is written into the cards rather than the base rules. Because of this, if I teach the game to some folks and they excitedly go off to play on their own and then run into the difficulty of having to figure out lots of details (Spite, Ennead as prime examples), I could see them being turned off. My impression, however, has been that enough people get excited enough about Sentinels that they're happy to put in the effort to understand that complexity.

I think this is going to be an issue of personal preference. The >G folks have done their analysis and come to a conclusion that it sounds like some folks are asking them to revisit. It has definitely been an interesting conversation. Personally, I really appreciate that you've all been so civil about it!

My thoughts are long and elaborate, and I haven't been able to make time to type them out. (Honestly, I shouldn't be doing it now, but I felt like it wasn't going to happen anytime soon, anyway so I might as well make it happen. )

When dealing with any kind of user interface (which is what we're talking about), the design has three audiences to consider: Novice, Experienced, and Expert. In this context, those of us who are used to gaming iconography are going to be experienced by default. In general, icons alienate novices, as they just don't know what they're supposed to do with it. (I often have this issue at work, where I need to ensure everyone understands what's being shown on a screen / document / presentation, but everyone has a different current level of understanding and experience.)

I shared Spiff's image of the side-by-side Frosthounds with a person who is an intelligent, casual gamer who has been playing Sentinels as long as (although admittedly not as much as) I have - since it was first released. I just told the person to take a look at the versions and let me know what they thought. The person glanced at the cards and immediately said "What's 'EV' mean?". I told them to read both cards, completely. They did, and said, "Okay, but what's 'EV' mean." I pointed to the "At the start of the villain turn" clause then at the "EV". Naturally, the person immediate understood the meaning, but without that side-by-side comparison it would require going through the rulebook and finding the information for them to get that, and that doesn't mean the person would immediately have gotten it nor that the person would have found the game as enjoyable if they were playing it that way for the first time.

My personal experience is that a lot of people just don't/can't think in symbols. There's nothing wrong with that, it's just an obstacle that we create when we require them to do so.

Theta_Sigma:

Trying to hit something of a middle ground here, but what about bolding key words? "At the start of the villain turn…"

Personally, on my made-up villain and environment, I've colored all the triggers (not just the key words, as that doesn't tend to stand out enough for us). Note: We don't have anyone in our play group who is color blind. This has really helped accellerate gameplay with these decks. I haven't bolded the phrases, yet, but I think I'm going to do that next. My only concern is that it might take up more room, and for some cards that might be an issue.

In general, I think something like this is far easier to manage and deal with. It helps the novices, in that they have nothing to reference, and it helps the experienced as they have something to glance at to find what they need.

The Start and End tokens make a huge difference, since so many of the triggers are based on these. It's the "oddities", the triggers like when a card is played, that are harder to remember. It's not like we're going to do something to review all the cards for triggers every time we do something. Personally, I have a bag of various kinds of tokens and dice that I use for this - if there's something that triggers on card draw, I put a bright and shiny token on my deck. If there's something that triggers on damage, I put a different one in my HP pile. Things like that that will remind me that something happens. Because these are so rare, it's easy enough to manage that way as there is likely few such triggers in play.

 

(Notice I never talk about experts. That's because they have all the cards memorized and don't need to read them anymore… )

The >G folks have done their analysis and come to a conclusion that it sounds like some folks are asking them to revisit.

I think it would be great if they ran actual user interface  experiments, like we do in software.  Mock up some cards both with and without simple icons and do two things:  (1) ask people which one they think would make the game easier to play, and then (2) watch them play with both to see which actually do make the game easier to play.  The results from (1) will be interesting, but the results from (2) will be the actual meat of what you want to know.

Novice, Experienced, and Expert.

I agree.  I think the Expert users should be consulted for their opinions, but not necessarily studied with UI experiments since, by definition, they're Experts, so they will likely be able to play the game smoothly regardless of whether text or icons are used.  But you should test how novices play and how experienced players play.  I can't imagine that icons will slow down or make either group of players have a diminished experience with the game, but without data, that's just an opinion.

I shared Spiff's image of the side-by-side Frosthounds with a person who is an intelligent, casual gamer who has been playing Sentinels as long as (although admittedly not as much as) I have - since it was first released. I just told the person to take a look at the versions and let me know what they thought. The person glanced at the cards and immediately said "What's 'EV' mean?".

Was your experiment with your friend to see if he could figure out what the icon meant without ever having read about it in a rule book once?  The first time you showed him the "H" symbol, could he immediately figure out what that one meant with no clues?  The best symbol is one that you can figure out without being told what it means, but the goal with these icons is to reduce the amount of reading and re-reading players need to do on a table full of cards.  You should only need to tell a player what the icon represents once for that goal to be met, I think.

No offense, Spiff, but playtesting is self-selecting experienced players - there are no novice players in the playtesting community. Yes, we're new to the cards, but we're experienced with gaming and/or SotM, so it removes the factor of new players. And I think that's where the concern with icons resides - at least, that's it for me.

Mind you, I am definitely not saying icons slow anyone down. (Has anyone actually said that? Not sure where that came from, but I might have missed it. )

I also don't think the current situation is optimal.

Here's my thoughts, as succinctly as I can:

  • Lack of method of easy trigger identification creates a delay in game play as players must review all cards at standard trigger points (e.g., end of turn, start of turn)
  • Lack of method of easy trigger identification creates missed play moments and issues with game play as players miss non-standard trigger points (e.g., card is destroyed, card is played)
  • Icons create an additional learning point in the game (with a short learning curve)
  • Icons reduce novice gamers interest in the game
 

I don't believe icons slow down the game, but they have other detriments that make them less favorable, in my opinion.

In playtesting, I've highlighted text as others have described. This resolved the situation for us - at start of turn, I glance at the board and can easily see all the green highlights. At end of turn, I glance at the board and can easily see all the red (okay, pink ) highlights. Now, we can't just highlight (colorblind players won't benefit from that) but it's definitely a start towards something easier and quicker.

My opinion is we should look at ways to make the current text more readily visible at a glance. This allows new players to see and read the full text without creating another learning point while still allowing players to glance at the cards and understand what is potentially triggered. It's not optimal, as the non-standard trigger points are still a potential issue, but just having them more visible will help keep them in players' minds.

Are there other options that might promote recognition of triggers?
